To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the predictive value of hypoxia markers for radiotherapy is still under debate and requires more clinical studies to be proven; (2) the predictive value for radiotherapy of DNA repair markers is not clear and requires more studies to be confirmed; (3) the predictive value in radiotherapy of cancer stem cell markers needs further investigation; and (4) the predictive value on radiotherapy of epidermal growth receptor inhibition markers needs more studies to be proven.

(1) hypoxia is a major factor that limits the effectiveness of radiotherapy; (2) hypoxia‐inducible factors are key players in the hypoxic response and may represent potential targets for the modulation of tumor radioresponse; (3) the combination of hypoxic radiosensitizer with radiotherapy is effective and may improve tumor control; (4) hypoxia may be a key player in the resistance to epidermal growth‐factor receptor inhibitors; (5)

the combination of hypoxia, DNA repair and metabolism is of high relevance to predict the response of tumors to radiotherapy, and that the use of monoclonal antibodies to target the epidermal receptor is of high relevance for the treatment of head and neck cancers.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following aspects: (1) the development and validation of new imaging and biological techniques for non‐invasive assessment of tumor oxygenation; (2) the development and clinical validation of novel radiotherapy treatment strategies for individualized radiotherapy; and (3) the development and application of novel molecular imaging and therapy techniques for personalized cancer treatment.
identifying and validating predictive biomarkers for radiation oncology.
the development of new methods for the individualization of radiation therapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no single biomarker that can be used to predict the radiotherapeutic response of an individual tumor.
we are still at a very early stage of biomarker development for individualized radiotherapy, but that the field is moving fast.
there are no predictive biomarkers available for the field of radiotherapy that have been validated in a clinical trial setting and have been adopted in clinical practice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a need for more and better biomarkers to individualize cancer treatment.
the use of molecular biomarkers in radiation oncology is a very promising approach to improve treatment outcome and to reduce treatment toxicity.
the current knowledge is still very limited and that the development of predictive biomarkers of radiotherapy response is a long way to go.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a great need for more translational research in radiation oncology.

there is a need for a better understanding of the biology of the tumor and its microenvironment, as well as of the interaction with the normal tissue in order to develop and validate predictive biomarkers.
the field of predictive biomarkers in radiotherapy is in its infancy, but has the potential to revolutionize radiotherapy in the future.
